title: Les voyelles nasales
intro: French has three nasal vowels — the air goes out through your nose. The **n** or **m** after the vowel is not pronounced: it's just a signal. Listen to each example, then hum it with your mouth open.

cases.label: /ɑ̃/ — an, am, en, em
cases.rule: **an, am, en, em** sound /ɑ̃/: *maman, chambre, enfant, temps*. Open mouth, like a deep “ah” through the nose.

cases.label: /ɔ̃/ — on, om
cases.rule: **on, om** sound /ɔ̃/: *bonjour, poisson, nom*. Round lips, like “oh” through the nose.

cases.label: /ɛ̃/ — in, ain, ein, un, ien
cases.rule: **in, im, ain, ein** sound /ɛ̃/: *vin, pain, plein*. **un** is /œ̃/ or /ɛ̃/ (most people now say /ɛ̃/). **ien** = /jɛ̃/: *bien, chien*.

cases.label: not nasal: n + vowel, nn, mm
cases.rule: If **n / m** is followed by a vowel, or doubled, the vowel is NOT nasal and you hear the n/m: *une, ami, banane, bonne, pomme, femme*.

cases.label: bon / bonne: masculine nasal, feminine not
cases.rule: Adding **-e** (or **-ne**) removes the nasal: *bon → bonne* /bɔ̃/ → /bɔn/, *fin → fine*, *cousin → cousine*.

cases.label: vent, vont, vin — different words
cases.rule: The three nasal vowels make different words: *vent* /vɑ̃/ (wind), *vont* /vɔ̃/ (they go), *vin* /vɛ̃/ (wine).

cases.label: nasals before a vowel
cases.rule: *un, mon, ton, son* keep the nasal and add /n/: *un‿ami* /œ̃.na.mi/. But **bon** loses it: *bon‿anniversaire* /bɔ.na.ni.vɛʁ.sɛʁ/.

sections.title: 1. /ɑ̃/ — an, am, en, em
sections.tip: **an** and **en** sound exactly the same: *cent* and *sans* (without) are both /sɑ̃/.

sections.title: 3. /ɛ̃/ — in, im, ain, ein, un, ien
sections.tip: **un** used to have its own sound (/œ̃/), and the voice in this app still says it that way. Today most people in France say it like *in*. Both are understood.

sections.title: 4. When it is NOT nasal
text: A vowel is nasal only if the **n / m** ends the syllable. If a vowel follows (*une, ami*), or the n/m is doubled (*bonne, pomme*), the vowel is normal and you hear the **n / m**.
sections.tip: In **banane** /ba.nan/, no vowel is nasal: each **n** is followed by a vowel.

examples.fr: Le pain est {bon|nas-pairs}, la soupe est {bonne|nas-pairs}.
examples.en: The bread is good, the soup is good.

sections.title: 7. Nasal vowels before a vowel
text: **un, mon, ton, son** keep their nasal vowel and add an /n/: *un‿ami* /œ̃.na.mi/, *mon‿amie* /mɔ̃.na.mi/. But **bon** loses its nasal: *bon‿anniversaire* /bɔ.na.ni.vɛʁ.sɛʁ/.

mistakes.why: Don't pronounce the **n** — it only makes the vowel nasal.
Different nasal vowels make different words.
Double **n**: not nasal, and you hear the n.

story.title: Le dimanche de l'oncle Jean
story.en: A short text full of nasal vowels. Listen, then read it aloud.

lines.fr: Le dimanche, mon {oncle|nas-on} Jean mange du {pain|nas-in} avec du {jambon|nas-on}.
lines.en: On Sundays, my uncle Jean eats bread with ham.
He drinks a good white wine.
His children are five and eleven.
They eat an apple and a banana.
The kitchen is full of good things.

lines.fr: Dehors, il y a du {vent|nas-minimal}, mais dedans, tout va {bien|nas-in}.
lines.en: Outside it's windy, but inside, all is well.

lines.fr: Aujourd'hui, c'est l'anniversaire de {son ami|nas-liaison} Simon.
lines.en: Today is his friend Simon's birthday.
